unit.title: Ship It: Web Craft with an AI Partner
unit.pitch: Build and ship a client website with an AI partner, from the first brief to the final handover.

blocks.html: The question
What is a website, and how does it exist?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Explain what a website physically is: files, a server, a URL, a repository, a deployment.
  2. Create a GitHub repository from the unit template and deploy a site.
  3. Direct an AI agent to produce a first version of a client site.
  4. Write a first SPEC.md that says what "done" means in your own words.
  5. Use the evidence trio: SPEC.md, DECISIONS.md, CRITIQUE.md.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour The deal, a live steer from one sentence to a deployed site, the client brief
Lab 2 hours Create the repo, meet the client, ship v0, write SPEC.md v0

There are no required pre-lab readings. The lecture and the lab carry the module.
The lab deliverable
A live URL a stranger can open on their phone, and SPEC.md v0. This is formative: it is not marked, but every later checkpoint builds on it.
The client

You are assigned one franchise of Harbour & Hearth, a small Perth cafe and bakery group. Your fact sheet has the business name, suburb, product mix, hours and one local quirk. The owner is Maria. The office manager is Dev. The customer is Sam. The IT vendor is Alex.

questions.prompt: What is the evidence trio you carry through the client project?
options: SPEC.md, DECISIONS.md and CRITIQUE.md
README.md, LICENSE and index.html
spec.md, quiz.md and notes.md
plan.md, build.md and deploy.md
questions.explanation: The three files record what was asked, what you changed and what you would do differently.

questions.prompt: What is the first marked checkpoint in the unit?
options: CP1.1, the 375px audit in Module 02
The A3 systems audit in the exam period
The A2 viva at the end of Module 11
The Module 01 deployment
questions.explanation: Module 01 is formative. The first marks come from the 375px audit in Module 02.

questions.prompt: What does Maria need the site to do?
options: Help people find the business, see the menu and book a table
Run an online store with payments and delivery
Replace her Facebook page and phone entirely
Rank first for every cafe search in Perth
questions.explanation: The brief is narrow on purpose. Find, see, book.

questions.prompt: What do you ship at the end of the Module 01 lab?
options: A live URL and SPEC.md v0
A finished A2 application
A deck of lecture slides
A marked portfolio
questions.explanation: A stranger can open the URL on a phone, and the spec says what done means.

blocks.html: The question
Why does it look fine on your laptop and break on a phone?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Explain the viewport meta tag and why it matters on a phone.
  2. Identify the common causes of horizontal scrolling and unreadable text.
  3. Use semantic landmarks and a heading hierarchy so a screen reader can navigate.
  4. Check focus visibility and keyboard reachability.
  5. Run an audit, name the cause precisely, and direct a fix.
  6. Write acceptance criteria that prevent the defect from returning.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour A live steer: the agent says "fully responsive". The phone disagrees
Lab 2 hours Audit your A1 site, name the causes, direct three fixes, present CP1.1
The lab deliverable
An audit table with at least five findings, three fixes as separate commits, and updated acceptance criteria in SPEC.md.

lessons.title: Name the cause before you fix it

blocks.html: The situation

Your client forwarded an email from a customer:

"Tried to book on my phone on the bus. Couldn't find the button. Gave up."

Your client's question: "Is the site broken?"

Your job: find out, prove it, explain it in words the client understands, and direct the fix.
Round 1: Find it (35 minutes)

1. Open your deployed site on your phone. Try the three most important customer tasks from SPEC.md v0. If you did not list any, use: find the opening hours, find how to get in touch, complete the main call to action.
  2. Open DevTools device mode at 375 x 667 and choose a slow network preset. Reload. Watch what loads and when.
  3. Turn on a screen reader. Navigate using headings and landmarks only. Can you reach the main call to action? Does every image announce something useful?
  4. Put your mouse away. Use the keyboard only (Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter). Can you always see where you are?
  5. Record every finding in CRITIQUE.md under ## 375px audit:
# What happened Where Evidence Who it affects
1 Booking button off-screen at 375px Home, hero screenshots/01-hero.png Phone users

Aim for at least five findings. Your agent is not allowed to help in this round. This round is your eyes.
Round 2: Name it (25 minutes)

For each finding, work out why it happens. Use your agent as a tutor, not a fixer:

"Explain why [finding] happens on this page. Point me to the file and line. Do not change any files."

Then confirm it yourself in the DevTools Elements panel. Add two columns:

# Cause (named precisely) File and line

The usual suspects: a missing viewport meta tag, fixed widths in pixels, images without max-width, divs where landmarks should be, missing or useless alt text, skipped heading levels, low contrast, and outline: none removing the focus ring.

questions.prompt: A page renders as a wide desktop layout on a 375px phone, so the text looks tiny. What is the cause?
options: The viewport meta tag is missing
The CSS uses flexbox
The images have alt text
The page has too many headings
questions.explanation: Without width=device-width the phone assumes a desktop viewport and scales the page down.

questions.prompt: The page scrolls sideways at 375px. What is the usual cause?
options: Fixed pixel widths on containers or images
A missing favicon
Too many CSS variables
A short page title
questions.explanation: A container fixed at 1200px stays 1200px wide. Use fluid widths with a max-width.

questions.prompt: Keyboard users cannot see which link they are on. What is the usual cause?
options: outline none on focus
Headings that skip a level
Images without width attributes
A missing lang attribute
questions.explanation: Removing the focus outline removes the only visible keyboard position cue.

questions.prompt: A screen reader user cannot jump straight to the page content. What is missing?
options: A main landmark and a logical heading order
A meta description
A table of contents
An animated hero image
questions.explanation: Landmarks and headings are the two navigation structures a screen reader user relies on.

questions.prompt: axe reports zero violations. Does that prove the page is accessible?
options: No. Automated checks miss meaning, order and usability
Yes. axe covers every accessibility rule
Yes, if the page also passes the HTML validator
Only if the page has no images
questions.explanation: A check can see a missing alt attribute. It cannot tell whether the alt text is useful or whether the task is possible.

questions.prompt: Which acceptance criterion prevents sideways scrolling from returning?
options: Every page works at 375px wide with no horizontal scroll
The site looks good on my laptop
Use a modern CSS framework
Add overflow-x hidden to the body
questions.explanation: A checkable criterion names the width and the observable result. overflow-x hidden hides the symptom.

blocks.html: The question
What does the client actually need?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Interview a stakeholder and separate what they say from what they need.
  2. Reconcile conflicting requirements from different people.
  3. Write a spec with information architecture, a content model, design tokens and checkable acceptance criteria.
  4. Run a replication test: give the spec alone to a fresh agent and measure the gap.
  5. Revise the spec, not the chat, until the replica converges.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour A live client interview, a spec written in front of the room, a replication test
Lab 2 hours Interview Dev and Sam, write SPEC.md v1, run the replication test, present CP1.2
The lab deliverable
SPEC.md v1, a replication test result, the gap recorded in CRITIQUE.md, and at least one spec revision caused by the test.
The situation

Maria wants a site. Dev updates the menu. Sam books on a phone. Alex worries about maintenance. They do not agree.

Your job is to find out what they actually need, write it down, and test whether the spec is good enough for a stranger to build from.
Round 1: Interview (25 minutes)

Interview Dev and Sam. Use the chatbot or the printed cards. Open with:

"I am the contractor for [franchise] in [suburb]. Here is my fact sheet: ..."

Ask:

  • What do you do today that the site should make easier?
  • What content changes, how often, and who changes it?
  • What device do you use, and where are you when you use it?
  • What would make you give up on the site?
  • What can the site not do?

Do not ask "what do you want on the site?" That produces a feature list. Ask about the task.

Done when: you have at least five concrete requirements and one conflict between two people.
Round 2: Write `SPEC.md` v1 (30 minutes)

Update your spec with:

  1. Purpose: one or two sentences from the client's point of view.
  2. Users and top tasks: a table with device and context.
  3. Content: pages, sections, and the content model.
  4. Must / Should / Won't: priorities, with the conflict resolved.
  5. Constraints: stack, devices, accessibility, performance, brand.
  6. Acceptance criteria: at least five, each checkable.
  7. Out of scope: what this version will not do.

Do not let the agent write the spec. It can ask you questions, but you write it.

Done when: a stranger could build from it without asking you what you meant.
Round 3: Replication test (25 minutes)

1. Create an empty folder outside your repo, for example ../replica.
  2. Open a fresh agent session with no context from your build.
  3. Give it only SPEC.md and the fact sheet. No screenshots, no links to your site.
  4. Ask it to build the site in the empty folder.
  5. Open the replica next to your site. Compare: - What is missing? - What is different? - Which difference is a spec problem, and which is a build problem?
  6. Record the result in CRITIQUE.md under ## Replication test:
Date Spec version Result Biggest gap Spec change made

Done when: you can name the one sentence that would have prevented the biggest gap.
Round 4: Revise the spec (20 minutes)

1. Add the missing sentence, acceptance criterion, or constraint.
  2. Do not change the chat. Change the spec.
  3. Update the version to v1.1 if the change is material.

Done when: the next replica would be closer, and you can say why.

questions.prompt: Dev says "add a gallery". What should you ask first?
options: What are you trying to do that the gallery would help with?
What colour should the gallery be?
Which JavaScript library should we use?
How many photos do you have?
questions.explanation: A feature request is not a requirement. Ask about the task behind it.

questions.prompt: Maria says the site must look "professional". What is the next move?
options: Turn it into checkable criteria with the client
Put it in the spec exactly as she said it
Ignore it because it cannot be measured
Ask the agent to decide what professional means
questions.explanation: Vague words are requirements in disguise. Convert them into something a stranger can test.

questions.prompt: Dev wants the menu first; Sam wants booking first. What do you do?
options: Record the conflict and the decision in DECISIONS.md
Pick one silently and move on
Put both first on every page
Ask the agent to break the tie
questions.explanation: Conflicts are evidence. Record who wanted what and why you decided as you did.

questions.prompt: What makes a replication test valid?
options: A fresh agent, an empty folder, and only SPEC.md and the fact sheet
Your current chat, your screenshots and your deployed site
The same agent that built the site
A second student reviewing your code
questions.explanation: The test measures the spec, so the builder must have nothing else to go on.

questions.prompt: The replica differs from your site. How do you tell a spec problem from a build problem?
options: Ask whether a stranger could have known the requirement from the spec alone
Assume every difference is the agent's fault
Assume every difference is your fault
Rebuild the replica until it matches
questions.explanation: If the spec did not say it, the replica could not know it. That is a spec problem.

questions.prompt: The replication test exposed a gap. Where does the fix go?
options: In the spec, then re-test
In the chat, then carry on
In DECISIONS.md only
In the replica's CSS
questions.explanation: The next person will not have your chat. Change the artefact that travels.

blocks.html: These are a draft spec's acceptance criteria. Each one sounds reasonable and none of them can be tested. Rewrite them so a stranger could run each check and give a clear pass or fail.

blocks.prompt:
Replace the draft with at least five numbered or bulleted acceptance criteria. Cover the essentials for this client:

  • a phone width and no horizontal scrolling
  • a booking action with a measurable outcome
  • the menu showing the current week
  • keyboard-only use
  • headings or landmarks
  • alt text

Remove vague words. "Professional", "modern", "simple", "fast" and "user-friendly" are not checks. Press Run tests when you have a draft.
blocks.starter:
Draft acceptance criteria (v0)

1. The site looks professional.
2. The menu is easy to update.
3. Booking is simple on mobile.
4. The site is accessible.
5. It loads fast.

tests.name: At least five criteria
tests.script:
const lines = text.split('\n').map((line) => line.trim()).filter((line) => /^([-*]|\d+[.)])\s+\S/.test(line));
assert(lines.length >= 5, 'Write at least five numbered or bulleted criteria. Found ' + lines.length + '.');

tests.name: No vague words
Width and horizontal scroll
tests.script:
const lines = text.split('\n');
assert(lines.some((line) => /375\s*px/i.test(line) && /(horizontal|sideways|scroll)/i.test(line)), 'Add a criterion that names 375px and rules out horizontal scrolling.');

tests.name: Booking has a measurable outcome
tests.script:
const lines = text.split('\n');
assert(lines.some((line) => /book/i.test(line) && /(minute|second|visible|tap|steps?)/i.test(line)), 'Say what a booking user must be able to do, and by when.');

tests.name: The menu is current
tests.script:
const lines = text.split('\n');
assert(lines.some((line) => /menu/i.test(line) && /(week|monday|current)/i.test(line)), 'Add a criterion for the menu showing the current week.');

tests.name: Keyboard only
tests.script:
const lines = text.split('\n');
assert(lines.some((line) => /keyboard/i.test(line)), 'Add a criterion that every task can be completed with a keyboard.');

tests.name: Headings or landmarks
tests.script:
const lines = text.split('\n');
assert(lines.some((line) => /\b(h1|heading|landmark)\b/i.test(line)), 'Add a criterion about the h1, heading order, or landmarks.');

tests.name: Alt text
tests.script:
const lines = text.split('\n');
assert(lines.some((line) => /\balt\b/i.test(line)), 'Add a criterion for meaningful alt text.');

hints: A criterion names the user, the action, and the result.
Works at 375px with no horizontal scroll is a check. "Looks good on mobile" is not.
The model spec in the unit uses six criteria. You can use exactly those.

blocks.html: The question
How do you know it works?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Explain the four WCAG principles and what each one asks of a page.
  2. Distinguish what automated checks catch from what a human still has to check.
  3. Write a Playwright check from an acceptance criterion.
  4. Read git log -- checks/ and prove the provided checks were not weakened.
  5. Direct a fix when a check fails, without letting the agent edit the check.
  6. Name one thing your checks still cannot see.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour Write a check live, watch the agent game it, name what checks miss
Lab 2 hours Run the checks, fix the site, write one new check, present CP1.3
The lab deliverable
npm test passing, or failures documented with reasons, plus one check you wrote from a SPEC.md acceptance criterion. The provided checks must be unchanged in git.
The situation

The agent says the site is done. The client has a customer with low vision who could not find the booking button. The site passed every automated check.

Your job: prove what works, find what the checks miss, and write one check that would have caught a real problem.
Round 1: Run the checks (20 minutes)

1. Run npm run check.
  2. Record every failure in CRITIQUE.md under ## Check results.
  3. Do not fix anything yet.
  4. Open the failing page at 375px and with a screen reader. Is the failure real?

Done when: you can list every failure and say whether it is a site problem or a check problem.
Round 2: Fix the site, not the checks (30 minutes)

1. Fix one failure at a time.
  2. Make one commit per fix.
  3. After each fix, run the check again.
  4. Record anything the agent changed that you did not ask for in DECISIONS.md.

Done when: the provided checks pass, or the remaining failures are documented with a reason.
Round 3: Write one check (30 minutes)

Choose one acceptance criterion from SPEC.md that the provided checks do not cover. Write a check in tests/, never in checks/.

Examples:

  • Every page has a non-empty title.
  • The booking form has a label for every input.
  • The primary action is reachable by keyboard.
  • The page has no heading level skipped.
  • The API failure shows a message, not a blank space.

Run it. Make it fail once on purpose, then fix the site.

Done when: your check fails when the criterion is false, and passes when it is true.
Round 4: Prove the checks were not weakened (15 minutes)

Run:

git log --oneline -- checks/

The only commit should be the one that added the checks. If the agent edited a check, revert it and record what happened in DECISIONS.md.

Done when: checks/ is unchanged since the template.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: evidence, not a green tick

questions.prompt: Which set is the four WCAG principles?
options: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
Perceivable, Readable, Usable, Secure
Visible, Clickable, Readable, Fast
Structure, Style, Behaviour, Data
questions.explanation: POUR. Each principle asks a different question of the page.

questions.prompt: The page passes axe with zero violations. Is it accessible?
options: Not necessarily. Automated checks cannot judge meaning or usability
Yes, axe covers every WCAG rule
Yes, if the HTML validator also passes
Only if the page has no images
questions.explanation: axe can find a missing alt attribute. It cannot tell whether the alt text is useful.

questions.prompt: Where should a check come from?
options: An acceptance criterion in the spec
The code the agent just wrote
The easiest element to select
A copy of the template check
questions.explanation: A check is evidence for a requirement. Start from the requirement, not the implementation.

questions.prompt: The agent made a failing check pass. What do you inspect first?
options: The diff. Did it fix the page or the check?
The commit message
The npm version
The browser zoom level
questions.explanation: Agents optimise for the green check. The diff tells you whether the page or the test changed.

questions.prompt: Which change is gaming the check?
options: Adding aria-hidden to the element that failed
Making the container fluid
Adding useful alt text
Fixing the heading order
questions.explanation: aria-hidden removes the problem from assistive technology instead of fixing it.

questions.prompt: Before you trust a new check, what must you do?
options: Make it fail on the broken page, then pass after the fix
Run it once and see green
Ask the agent to confirm it is correct
Add a fixed wait so it is stable
questions.explanation: A check that has never failed has not proven it can catch anything.

questions.prompt: What can an automated check still not see?
options: Whether the alt text is meaningful and the copy is clear
Whether a heading element exists
Whether an image has an alt attribute
Whether the page returns HTTP 200
questions.explanation: Structure is checkable. Meaning, clarity and usability need a human.

blocks.html:
A check is evidence for one acceptance criterion. Write a Playwright check for the criterion below. The tests inspect the shape and safety of your check, not a live browser.

Criterion: the booking action is visible at 375px without scrolling. The booking control is [data-cta="primary"].

blocks.prompt:
Write the check in tests/, never in checks/.

Your check must:

  • import test and expect from @playwright/test
  • set the viewport to 375px wide
  • navigate with await page.goto(...)
  • find [data-cta="primary"] with page.locator(...)
  • assert it is in the viewport, not merely visible in the DOM
  • avoid test.skip, test.fixme and test.only
  • avoid hiding the problem with overflow: hidden or display: none

tests.name: Imports test and expect
tests.script:
assert(/@playwright\/test/.test(text), 'Import from @playwright/test.');
assert(/\btest\b/.test(text) && /\bexpect\b/.test(text), 'Import both test and expect.');

tests.name: Has a named test
tests.script: assert(/test\s*\(\s*['"`][^'"`]+['"`]/.test(text), 'Call test() with a description string.');

tests.name: Sets a 375px viewport
tests.script:
assert(/375/.test(text), 'Set the viewport width to 375.');
assert(/setViewportSize|viewport/i.test(text), 'Use page.setViewportSize or test.use with a viewport.');

tests.name: Navigates with await page.goto
tests.script: assert(/await\s+page\.goto\s*\(/.test(text), 'Navigate with await page.goto("/").');

tests.name: Uses the booking locator
tests.script: assert(/locator\s*\(\s*['"`]\[data-cta=["']?primary/.test(text), 'Find the booking control with page.locator(\'[data-cta="primary"]\').');

tests.name: Asserts it is in the viewport
tests.script:
assert(/toBeInViewport|boundingBox/.test(text), 'Assert the call to action is in the viewport, not just present in the DOM.');
assert(/await\s+expect\s*\(/.test(text), 'Use await expect(...) for the assertion.');

tests.name: Does not skip or focus the test
tests.script: assert(!/test\.(skip|fixme|only)/.test(text), 'Remove test.skip, test.fixme or test.only.');

tests.name: Does not hide the problem
tests.script: assert(!/overflow\s*:\s*hidden|display\s*:\s*none/.test(text), 'Fix the layout. Do not hide the element or the overflow.');

hints: Set the viewport before you navigate.
Playwright's toBeVisible checks CSS visibility. toBeInViewport checks that the element is actually on screen.
The check should fail on the broken page. If it passes immediately, it is not testing the criterion.

blocks.prompt: The agent was asked to make a failing check pass. Click the lines that changed the evidence instead of the page.

lines.code: test('booking action is visible at 375px', async ({ page }) => {

lines.feedback: The assertion that proves the criterion was removed.
This hides the control from assistive technology. It does not make it visible.

blocks.explanation: The check stopped testing the criterion. Revert the test and fix the layout so the booking control is in the viewport.

blocks.html: The question
Where does the data come from, and who can see it?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Explain the difference between client and server, and what a user can see.
  2. Use fetch with async/await to retrieve JSON.
  3. Move a request that needs a secret into a serverless function.
  4. Use an environment variable and keep the key out of the repository.
  5. Handle the unhappy path: loading, error and empty states.
  6. Write a check that mocks a failed API response.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour Add a live data widget, find the key in View Source, move it to a function, break the API
Lab 2 hours Integrate an API, move it server-side, add the unhappy path, present CP1.4
The lab deliverable
Live data in the site, no secret in client code, loading/error/empty states, a failing-API check, and a DECISIONS.md entry.

lessons.title: Data, secrets and the unhappy path

blocks.html: The situation

The client wants live data on the site. The supplier's API needs a key. The site is public. If the key is in the browser, anyone can take it.

Your job: integrate the data, keep the secret on the server, and make the site behave sensibly when the API fails.
Round 1: Fetch the data (25 minutes)

1. Choose one public API. Read its documentation.
  2. Fetch it from a page. Show the data in a simple list or table.
  3. Record the request and response in DECISIONS.md: URL, method, status, shape.
  4. Do not use a key yet.

Done when: the data appears on the page and you can explain the JSON shape.
Round 2: Move it to a serverless function (25 minutes)

1. Create a function in netlify/functions/ (or the Cloudflare equivalent).
  2. Move the fetch into the function.
  3. Return JSON from the function.
  4. Fetch the function from the page.
  5. If the API needs a key, read it from an environment variable. Never put it in site/.

Done when: the page still shows the data and the key is not in the browser.
Round 3: The unhappy path (25 minutes)

Add three states:

  • Loading: a message or skeleton while the request is in flight.
  • Error: a friendly message when the request fails, with a way to retry.
  • Empty: a message when the API returns no data.

Test each one. Turn off the network, use a wrong URL, and return an empty array.

Done when: the page never shows a blank space or a spinner that never stops.
Round 4: A failing-API check (20 minutes)

Write a Playwright test in tests/ that mocks a 500 response and asserts that the page shows a friendly message.

await page.route('**/.netlify/functions/rates*', route =>
  route.fulfill({ status: 500, body: 'error' })
);

Done when: the check fails if the error message is missing.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: who can see the key?

questions.prompt: Where can a browser user read an API key that is embedded in client-side JavaScript?
options: Anywhere. View Source, DevTools and the network tab all show it
Nowhere, if the file is minified
Only if they have the repository
Only on the production site, not locally
questions.explanation: The browser must download and run the code, so the user can read it. Minifying does not hide it.

questions.prompt: Where should a key that the browser must not see live?
options: A server-side environment variable, read by a function
A constant at the top of app.js
A hidden input in the HTML
A comment in the CSS
questions.explanation: The server can hold a secret. Anything the browser receives is public.

questions.prompt: You deleted the key from the current file. Are you safe?
options: No. It is still in git history. Rotate it and clean the history
Yes. The file no longer contains it
Yes, if the repository is private
No, you must also add it to .gitignore
questions.explanation: A deleted line is still in earlier commits. Rotate the key, then remove it from history.

questions.prompt: The API is down. What should the page show?
options: A friendly message and a way to retry
A blank space where the widget was
A spinner that keeps going
The browser's raw network error
questions.explanation: Loading, error and empty are three different states. The user needs to know what happened and what to do.

questions.prompt: Which check proves the unhappy path works?
options: A Playwright test that mocks a 500 and asserts the message
A manual click on the happy path
A screenshot of the loading state
A check that the HTTP server is running
questions.explanation: Mock the failure and assert the user-visible result. That is the only way to know the error state exists.

questions.prompt: Why is `innerHTML` with API data risky?
options: It can inject untrusted markup and scripts. Use textContent
It is slower than textContent in every browser
It strips all styles from the page
It stops fetch from working
questions.explanation: API data is untrusted input. Setting innerHTML lets that input become active markup.

The question
Which build would the client pay for?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Judge a build against the client's brief, not your own taste.
  2. Use a performance budget and Lighthouse to find the biggest cost.
  3. Fix layout shift and oversized images.
  4. Write a critique that chooses, not just lists.
  5. Explain any commit in your repository and defend one override.
  6. Submit a complete A1 portfolio and pass the viva.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour Two builds, same spec, both pass checks. Critique and performance
Lab 2 hours Critique pairs, finalise CRITIQUE.md, viva readiness, final submission
Viva Booked slot 10 minutes, screen shared, code open
The lab deliverable
A final A1 site, a complete CRITIQUE.md, and viva readiness. The final submission is due at the end of the module.
The situation
The client has two quotes for the same brief. Both sites pass every check. One is clearly better. Your job is to say why, in language the client understands.
Round 1: Critique pairs (30 minutes)

1. Pair with a classmate. Swap URLs.
  2. Open the other site on a phone.
  3. Try the three top tasks from the other student's SPEC.md.
  4. Compare it with your site against the same brief.
  5. Write three findings: one strength, one defect, one judgement call.

Done when: you can say which site you would pay for, and why, without referring to your own preferences.
Round 2: Finalise `CRITIQUE.md` (30 minutes)

Write:

  1. Would you charge money for this? Yes or no, and why, in a paragraph.
  2. The first three things you would change. Ordered, with a reason each.
  3. What you compared it with. The other site, a competitor, or a replica.
  4. What you still do not understand. Be honest.

Done when: the critique chooses, not just lists.
Round 4: Viva readiness (20 minutes)

1. Open your commit history.
  2. Pick any commit. Explain in 30 seconds: what changed, why, what else it could affect.
  3. Pick one DECISIONS.md entry. Explain what you overrode and why.
  4. Ask your partner one question about their code.

Done when: you can explain any commit without preparation.

questions.prompt: Two builds pass every check. How do you decide which is better?
options: Judge both against the client's brief and top tasks
Pick the one with the higher Lighthouse score
Pick the one you would use yourself
Pick the one with more features
questions.explanation: The brief is the standard. Personal taste and a single score are not.

questions.prompt: What is a performance budget?
options: A limit you choose before you build, such as LCP under 2.5 seconds
The amount of money the client will pay
The number of pages in the site
The maximum number of commits
questions.explanation: A budget turns performance into a target you can design and test against.

questions.prompt: What is the usual cause of a hero image shifting the page as it loads?
options: The image has no width and height, so no space is reserved
The image has alt text
The page uses a stylesheet
The image loads eagerly
questions.explanation: Without explicit dimensions the browser does not know how much space to reserve. The content jumps when the image arrives.

questions.prompt: What does `srcset` do?
options: Offers several image files so the browser can choose by viewport and pixel density
Compresses the image automatically
Loads every image at once
Replaces the need for alt text
questions.explanation: srcset is a menu, not a download list. With sizes, the browser picks the smallest file that fits.

questions.prompt: A page scores 100 for performance in Lighthouse. Is that enough?
options: No. Lab scores vary, and field data and the user's task still matter
Yes. Lighthouse is the standard the client cares about
Yes, if the accessibility score is also 100
No, because Lighthouse only checks CSS
questions.explanation: A lab score is one run on one machine. It does not prove the customer can book on a bus.

questions.prompt: A critique lists ten problems. What is missing?
options: A choice about what matters most and why
More problems
A screenshot of each problem
A higher Lighthouse score
questions.explanation: A critique chooses. A list leaves the decision to the client.

questions.prompt: In the viva, what should you say about a commit?
options: What changed, why, and what else it could affect
Who wrote it and when
How many lines it changed
Which branch it is on
questions.explanation: The examiner wants your understanding, not the commit metadata.

blocks.html: The hero is an 800 x 600 JPEG served as one large file. It has no explicit dimensions, so the page shifts as it loads, and it renders wider than a phone. Fix the markup so the browser reserves space, chooses a sensible file, and keeps the hero inside a 375px screen.

blocks.prompt:
Update the img element:

  • add numeric width and height
  • add a srcset with at least two width descriptors
  • add a sizes attribute
  • load the hero eagerly, because it is the largest image on the page
  • write alt text that describes the image
  • point src at a sized file such as hero-800.jpg
  • keep the hero inside the 375px preview without horizontal scrolling

The preview is sandboxed and the image files do not exist, but the attributes and layout are real.
blocks.starter:
Harbour & Hearth

Fresh bread in Northbridge.

tests.name: Width and height reserve space
srcset offers at least two widths
sizes describes the display width

const img = doc.querySelector('img');
assert((img.getAttribute('sizes') || '').trim().length > 0, 'Add a sizes attribute so the browser knows how wide the image will display.');

tests.name: The hero loads eagerly
The alt text describes the image
src points at a sized file

const img = doc.querySelector('img');
assert(/-\d{3,4}\.(jpe?g|png|webp|avif)$/i.test(img.getAttribute('src') || ''), 'Point src at a sized file such as hero-800.jpg, not the original.');

tests.name: The hero fits a 375px screen

hints: width and height do not have to be the display size. They set the aspect ratio so the space is reserved.
srcset is a menu and sizes is the instruction. Together the browser picks a file.
The hero is the largest contentful paint. Do not lazy-load it.
CSS max-width 100% and height auto stops the image overflowing.

blocks.html: The question
Who maintains this on Monday?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Explain what a content management system is and why a business might need one.
  2. Separate content from presentation.
  3. Compare platforms on total cost of ownership, not on novelty.
  4. Explain lock-in and exit cost.
  5. Run a timeboxed spike and write a decision record.
  6. Choose a platform before you build, and justify it against the client's needs.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour The agent chooses a stack. Who maintains it? Then constrain it to WordPress
Lab 2 hours Three timeboxed spikes, a comparison, a decision record, an issue board
The lab deliverable
A decision record that compares at least three platforms against the client's needs, and an issue board for Sprint 1.
The situation

The business has grown. Dev must edit the menu herself. Customers want to book online. Maria has promised a launch. The A1 site is too small.

Your job: compare three ways to build the next version, choose one, and justify it against the client's needs.
Round 1: Static spike (25 minutes)

1. Take your A1 site as the baseline.
  2. Make the three changes the growth brief requires: Dev edits the menu, online booking, a staff page.
  3. Timebox it. Do not perfect it.
  4. Record what was easy, what was hard, and what you could not do.
  5. Take one screenshot.

Done when: you can say what a static site cannot give Dev.
Round 2: WordPress spike (25 minutes)

1. Create a local WordPress site in LocalWP. Use Playground or InstaWP only as a fallback.
  2. Create a menu content type or a menu page.
  3. Add two menu items. Edit one as if you were Dev.
  4. Find the REST API endpoint for your content.
  5. Record what was easy, what was hard, and what you could not do.

Done when: you can show Dev editing the menu without touching code.
Round 3: AI app builder or React spike (25 minutes)

1. Use an AI app builder, or a React starter, to build one view of the same content.
  2. Record what was easy, what was hard, and what you could not do.
  3. Do not try to finish it. The spike is a comparison, not a build.

Done when: you can say what this option costs in time and maintenance.
Round 4: Compare and decide (25 minutes)

1. Open the decision record template.
  2. Fill in the criteria table: staff editing, three-year cost, mobile, accessibility effort, lock-in, exit cost.
  3. Write the decision in one sentence, with the main reason.
  4. Write the consequences: what becomes easier, what becomes harder, what you accept.
  5. Write the review trigger: what would make you revisit this.
  6. Record whether you will migrate the A1 content or rebuild from the brief.

Done when: the decision is traceable to the client's needs, not to the agent's preference.
Round 5: Start the issue board (10 minutes)

1. Create 5-8 issues for Sprint 1.
  2. Each issue has an acceptance criterion and a size of one session or less.
  3. Put them in a simple board: to do, doing, done.
  4. Reference the issues in your commits.

Done when: the board reflects the sprint, not a wish list.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: the platform is your call

questions.prompt: What is a content management system?
options: A system where content is data that staff can edit without code
A code editor with syntax highlighting
A tool that compresses images
A hosting company that manages servers
questions.explanation: The CMS separates the content from the templates, so an office manager can update the menu.

questions.prompt: In the cafe example, what is content and what is presentation?
options: The menu text is content; the layout and colours are presentation
The layout is content; the menu text is presentation
Both are content because they appear on the page
Both are presentation because a browser renders them
questions.explanation: Content is what the business says. Presentation is how it is shown.

questions.prompt: What does total cost of ownership include?
options: Build, hosting, maintenance, updates and the cost of leaving
Only the build
Only the monthly hosting fee
Only the developer's hourly rate
questions.explanation: The cheapest build can be the most expensive platform over three years.

questions.prompt: What is lock-in?
options: What it costs in money, time and risk to move to another platform
A password that locks the admin account
A plugin that stops updates
A contract that forbids changes
questions.explanation: Exit cost is part of the decision. A platform you cannot leave is a risk.

questions.prompt: The agent chose Next.js with a headless CMS. What do you ask next?
options: Who maintains it on Monday, what it costs over three years, and how hard is it to leave?
Which version of Next.js it used?
Whether it can add animations?
How many files it created?
questions.explanation: The platform decision belongs to whoever owns the maintenance and the budget.

questions.prompt: What is the point of a timeboxed spike?
options: To compare options with evidence, not to finish a build
To produce the final application
To test the client's internet connection
To benchmark the laptop
questions.explanation: A spike buys enough evidence to decide. Perfecting it defeats the timebox.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a decision record?
options: Context, options, criteria, decision, consequences and a review trigger
A feature list and a screenshot
The agent's chat transcript
The final code only
questions.explanation: The record must let someone later see why the choice was made and when to revisit it.

blocks.html: The question
What did the previous developer leave?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Audit a WordPress site: plugins, versions, theme, users and API exposure.
  2. Explain how plugins and themes extend WordPress.
  3. Read a small plugin and look for nonces, sanitisation, escaping and capability checks.
  4. Decide what to keep, remove and replace, and justify it.
  5. Write handover notes that the next person can use.
  6. Review one agent-built plugin for security.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour Audit a messy WordPress site live, build a small plugin, read the PHP
Lab 2 hours Sprint 1 reviews, audit the provided site, build and review a plugin
The lab deliverable
A Sprint 1 review, handover notes in CRITIQUE.md, and a security review of one plugin.
The situation

The client's previous developer left. There are no handover notes. The site is live, the plugins are old, and the client wants a relaunch.

Your job: audit the site, decide what to keep, and write the handover the last person did not.
Round 2: Audit the provided site (30 minutes)

Record findings in CRITIQUE.md under ## Inherited site audit:

Area What to check Finding Risk
Plugins Versions, last update, unused
Theme Direct edits, child theme
Users Accounts that should not exist
API /wp-json/wp/v2/users and other endpoints
Content Out-of-date pages, missing alt
Performance Large images, render-blocking

Done when: you have at least eight findings with a risk rating.
Round 3: Build a small plugin (25 minutes)

Direct the agent to build a plugin with:

  • A settings page for opening hours.
  • A shortcode that displays the hours.
  • A capability check on the settings page.
  • A nonce on the form.
  • Sanitised input and escaped output.

Read the PHP. Do not accept it because it works.

Done when: you can point to the nonce, the sanitisation, the escaping and the capability check, or explain what is missing.
Round 4: Security review (10 minutes)

Answer four questions in CRITIQUE.md:

  1. Is there a nonce on the form?
  2. Is the input sanitised?
  3. Is the output escaped?
  4. Is there a capability check?

Add one thing you would change before installing it on a live site.

Done when: the review is specific, not a checklist.
Round 5: Record and hand over (5 minutes)

1. Add the top three findings to DECISIONS.md with what you would do.
  2. Write a short handover note: what you would keep, remove and replace.

questions.prompt: What does `/wp-json/wp/v2/users` expose on a default WordPress site?
options: User accounts and display names to anonymous requests
Only the administrator's password hash
Nothing, because the endpoint requires a login
A list of installed plugins
questions.explanation: The REST API can list users publicly unless it is restricted. That helps an attacker enumerate accounts.

questions.prompt: A theme was edited directly, with no child theme. Why is that a risk?
options: An update can overwrite the customisations
The theme cannot be activated
WordPress refuses to load it
It stops plugins from working
questions.explanation: Direct edits live inside the theme, so the next update replaces them. A child theme keeps the customisations separate.

questions.prompt: A plugin works. What four security checks do you make before installing it?
options: Nonce, sanitisation, escaping and capability checks
Colours, fonts, icons and layout
Version, author, licence and download count
Speed, size, cache and minification
questions.explanation: Working is not the same as safe. Read the PHP for those four things.

questions.prompt: What is a nonce for?
options: Confirming that a form submission came from the site and the user intended it
Encrypting the saved option
Hiding the admin menu from other users
Compressing the form data
questions.explanation: A nonce protects against cross-site request forgery. It is not encryption.

questions.prompt: Where do sanitisation and escaping belong?
options: Sanitise input when it is saved, escape output when it is shown
Escape input and sanitise output
Only sanitise input
Only escape input
questions.explanation: Clean the data on the way in, then escape it for the context on the way out.

questions.prompt: Which finding belongs in a handover as a launch blocker?
options: The domain is registered to the previous developer's email
The footer uses a serif font
A slider plugin is installed but unused
The blog has three old posts
questions.explanation: If the client does not control the domain, they do not control the site. That blocks launch.

questions.prompt: What should a handover note say?
options: What to keep, remove and replace, plus what must happen before launch
Everything the previous developer did wrong
A complete rewrite plan only
The plugin download links
questions.explanation: The next person needs decisions and blockers, not blame.

blocks.html:
A previous developer left this WordPress plugin. It registers a setting, renders a settings form and exposes a shortcode. It works. It is not safe.

Fix the PHP so it meets the four checks: capability, nonce, sanitisation and escaping.

blocks.prompt:
Rewrite the plugin. Keep the same feature: opening hours, a settings page and an [opening_hours] shortcode.

Add:

  1. a capability check with current_user_can('manage_options')
  2. a nonce with settings_fields('hh_settings')
  3. a sanitise callback with sanitize_text_field
  4. escaped output with esc_attr in the input and esc_html in the shortcode

Do not echo or return the option raw. The tests inspect your PHP for each control. They do not run it.

tests.name: Capability check on the settings page
tests.script: assert(/current_user_can\s*\(\s*['"]manage_options['"]\s*\)/.test(text), 'Add current_user_can(\'manage_options\') before rendering the settings page.');

tests.name: The form has a nonce
tests.script: assert(/settings_fields\s*\(\s*['"]hh_settings['"]\s*\)|wp_nonce_field\s*\(|check_admin_referer\s*\(/.test(text), 'Add a nonce with settings_fields(\'hh_settings\').');

tests.name: The option is sanitised on save
tests.script:
assert(/sanitize_callback/.test(text), 'Add a sanitize_callback to register_setting.');
assert(/sanitize_text_field|sanitize_textarea_field/.test(text), 'Sanitise the hours with sanitize_text_field.');

tests.name: The input value is escaped
tests.script: assert(/esc_attr\s*\(\s*get_option/.test(text), 'Escape the input value with esc_attr(get_option(...)).');

tests.name: The shortcode output is escaped
tests.script: assert(/esc_html\s*\(\s*get_option|wp_kses_post\s*\(\s*get_option/.test(text), 'Escape the shortcode output with esc_html(get_option(...)).');

tests.name: No raw option output
tests.script: assert(!/echo\s+get_option|return\s+get_option\s*\(/.test(text), 'Do not echo or return the option raw. Escape it first.');

settings_fields() adds the nonce and the option page fields.
Sanitise on the way in, escape on the way out.
The shortcode should return a string containing esc_html(get_option(...)), not the option itself.

Who can see the data?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Explain REST endpoints, resources and JSON shape.
  2. Expose a custom content type through the WordPress REST API.
  3. Fetch and present business data in the front end.
  4. Check what the site exposes publicly.
  5. Decide what should be private, and why.

This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour Expose a content type, fetch it, present it, inspect what a stranger can see
Lab 2 hours Integrate business data, check exposure, decide what is private
The lab deliverable
One business data set served through the REST API and presented in the front end, plus a short exposure review.
The situation

The client wants a staff-only dashboard of bookings or enquiries. The site already exposes more than it should. Your job: present the data the customer needs, protect the data the customer should not see, and record the decision.
Round 1: Expose the data (30 minutes)

1. Choose one business data set: the menu, the bookings, the enquiries, or the staff.
  2. Create a custom post type or a field group with show_in_rest enabled.
  3. Add three sample items.
  4. Open the endpoint in the browser: /wp-json/wp/v2/[type].
  5. Record the JSON shape in DECISIONS.md.

Done when: the endpoint returns the three items and you can explain the shape.
Round 2: Fetch and present (30 minutes)

1. Fetch the endpoint from the front end.
  2. Present it as a table or a chart. Choose based on the task.
  3. Add loading, error and empty states.
  4. Test with the API down.

Done when: the data displays, and the page behaves when the API fails.
Round 3: Exposure review (20 minutes)

Open these and record what a stranger can see:

  • /wp-json/wp/v2/users
  • /wp-json/wp/v2/[your-type]
  • Any custom endpoint you added.

Record in CRITIQUE.md under ## API exposure:

Endpoint What it exposes Should it be public? Action

Done when: you can name every public endpoint and say whether it should be.
Round 4: Decide what is private (20 minutes)

1. For each data set, decide: public, authenticated, or server-only.
  2. If it is private, explain how you protect it.
  3. If you cannot protect it today, record it as a known issue.
  4. Add the decision to DECISIONS.md.

Done when: the decision is explicit, not "the API does it".

questions.prompt: What does `show_in_rest` do on a custom post type?
options: Exposes the type through the WordPress REST API
Shows the type in the admin menu only
Makes the type searchable on the front end
Turns on the block editor
questions.explanation: Without show_in_rest the endpoint does not exist. With it, the collection becomes a public URL unless you restrict it.

questions.prompt: What is a resource in a REST API?
options: A thing addressed by a URL and returned as a representation such as JSON
A CSS file served by the server
A database table with no URL
A user permission
questions.explanation: REST maps resources to URLs. The JSON shape tells you what the resource contains.

questions.prompt: Which default endpoint can list WordPress users to an anonymous request?
options: /wp-json/wp/v2/users
/wp-json/wp/v2/settings
/wp-json/wp/v2/media
/feed
questions.explanation: The users endpoint can leak account names unless it is restricted.

questions.prompt: Should the bookings endpoint, with customer names and phone numbers, be public?
options: No. Authenticate it or keep it server-only
Yes, because the site is public
Yes, if the page has no login link
Yes, as long as the IDs are hidden
questions.explanation: Public by default is not a decision. Private data needs a gate.

questions.prompt: When should you present data as a chart rather than a table?
options: When the task is to see a trend or comparison over time
When there are many exact values to look up
When the data has more than three columns
Always, because charts look better
questions.explanation: The task decides the form. Tables suit lookup and precision; charts suit trend and shape.

questions.prompt: The API returns an empty array. What should the page do?
options: Show a clear empty state, not a blank space
Show a spinner forever
Show the error message
Hide the whole page
questions.explanation: Empty is a state, separate from loading and error. Say that there is nothing yet.

questions.prompt: The API is public, so it is fine. What is wrong with that reasoning?
options: Public by default is not a decision. Decide who needs the data and protect the rest
Nothing. Public endpoints are always safe
It is fine if the endpoint has a long URL
It is fine if the data is in JSON
questions.explanation: Exposure is a choice. Name every endpoint and decide its audience.

blocks.html: The question
Does the client need an app?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Explain what makes a web app installable.
  2. Write a web app manifest and a minimal service worker.
  3. Design an offline state that makes sense for the business.
  4. Test installability on a real phone.
  5. Compare a PWA with an app-store app and a native app on cost, updates and reach.
  6. Present the Sprint 2 review.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour Make a site installable, switch to airplane mode, compare with an app
Lab 2 hours Sprint 2 reviews, manifest, service worker, offline state, install on a phone
The lab deliverable
A Sprint 2 review, an installable app, and a sensible offline state.
The situation
The client asks for an app. The customers are on phones. The budget is small. Your job: give them an installable experience, a sensible offline state, and a recommendation about the app store.
Round 2: Manifest (30 minutes)

1. Create site/manifest.webmanifest.
  2. Add name, short name, start URL, display, theme colour, background colour.
  3. Add 192px and 512px icons.
  4. Link it from every page.
  5. Check the Application panel in DevTools.

Done when: the browser offers to install the site.
Round 3: Service worker (25 minutes)

1. Create site/sw.js.
  2. Cache the app shell: the HTML, CSS, JS and icons.
  3. Use network-first for data, cache-first for the shell.
  4. Add an offline fallback page.
  5. Register the worker in main.js.

Done when: the app loads the shell when the network is off.
Round 4: Offline state (10 minutes)

1. Switch the phone to airplane mode.
  2. Open the installed app.
  3. Check what still works and what does not.
  4. Make the offline message useful: what can the user do now?

Done when: the offline state is a deliberate design, not a browser error.
Round 5: Install and test (10 minutes)

1. Install the app on a phone.
  2. Add it to the home screen.
  3. Open it offline.
  4. Record one thing that surprised you.

Done when: the app installs and the offline behaviour is documented.

questions.prompt: What does a web app need before a phone offers to install it?
options: HTTPS, a manifest with name, start URL, display and 192/512 icons, and a service worker
A React build and an app store listing
A native wrapper and a signing certificate
A separate mobile domain
questions.explanation: The browser checks the manifest, the icons, the start URL and a service worker over HTTPS.

questions.prompt: Which manifest display value opens the app without browser chrome?
options: standalone
browser
minimal-ui
fullscreen is the only option
questions.explanation: standalone gives an app-like window. fullscreen is an option but is not required.

questions.prompt: What does a service worker do?
options: Intercepts network requests and can serve cached responses
Styles the app for small screens
Compiles JavaScript for the phone
Stores the database on the server
questions.explanation: The worker sits between the page and the network. That is what makes the shell work offline.

questions.prompt: Which caching strategy suits the app shell and which suits business data?
options: Cache-first for the shell, network-first for data
Network-first for the shell, cache-first for data
Cache everything forever
Never cache anything
questions.explanation: The shell changes rarely, so cache it. Data changes often, so try the network first.

questions.prompt: Offline, the installed app shows the browser's error page. What is wrong?
options: The offline state was not designed. Add a fallback that says what still works
The phone has no manifest
The icons are the wrong size
The site is not on HTTPS
questions.explanation: Offline is a state to design. A browser error is the absence of a design.

questions.prompt: Why might a PWA beat an app-store app for this client?
options: One codebase, instant updates and no store fee or review
It has more features than native
It is always faster than native
It does not need HTTPS
questions.explanation: Reach and cost favour the web for a small business. Native wins when it needs deep device features.

questions.prompt: The client says "we should put it in the store". What do you ask?
options: What does the store give this client that the web does not?
Which store has the best icon?
How many screenshots should we take?
Which framework is most modern?
questions.explanation: A store adds review, fees and release friction. It needs a reason tied to the client's reach or device needs.

blocks.html:
The client wants the site to install on a phone. Write the web app manifest for Harbour & Hearth Northbridge.

The icons live at /icons/icon-192.png and /icons/icon-512.png.

blocks.prompt:
Write valid JSON for manifest.webmanifest. Include:

  • name and short_name
  • start_url set to /
  • display set to standalone
  • theme_color and background_color
  • an icons array with 192x192 and 512x512 PNG icons

The tests parse your JSON and check the install fields. Do not wrap it in markdown fences.

tests.name: The manifest is valid JSON
Name and short name are set
Start URL and display are set
Theme and background colours are set
Both icon sizes are present
The icon paths are usable

hints: A manifest without a 192px and a 512px icon will not install.
short_name is what the phone shows under the icon. Keep it short.
start_url should be a path on the site, not a full URL to another domain.

blocks.html:
Write the service worker that makes the shell load offline.

Cache the shell: /, /menu.html, /css/styles.css, /js/main.js and /offline.html. Use cache-first for the shell. For /wp-json/ requests, try the network, then fall back to /offline.html.

blocks.prompt:
Write sw.js and include the registration snippet for main.js.

Your worker must:

  • listen for install and cache the shell with cache.addAll
  • listen for activate and delete old caches
  • listen for fetch
  • serve the shell cache-first
  • try the network first for /wp-json/ and fall back to /offline.html
  • register the worker with navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')
blocks.starter:
// sw.js
// Cache the shell, handle fetch, and register at the bottom.

tests.name: Registers the service worker
tests.script: assert(/serviceWorker\.register\s*\(\s*['"]\/sw\.js['"]\s*\)/.test(text), 'Register the worker with navigator.serviceWorker.register(\'/sw.js\').');

tests.name: Caches the shell on install
Cleans old caches on activate
tests.script:
assert(/addEventListener\s*\(\s*['"]activate['"]/.test(text), 'Add an activate listener.');
assert(/caches\.delete/.test(text), 'Delete caches that are not the current version.');

tests.name: Handles fetch
tests.script:
assert(/addEventListener\s*\(\s*['"]fetch['"]/.test(text), 'Add a fetch listener.');
assert(/caches\.match|cache\.match/.test(text), 'Serve the shell from the cache.');

tests.name: Treats the API as network-first
tests.script:
assert(/wp-json/.test(text), 'Handle /wp-json/ requests separately.');
assert(/(wp-json[\s\S]{0,300}offline\.html)|(offline\.html[\s\S]{0,300}wp-json)/i.test(text), 'For API requests, try the network and fall back to offline.html.');

tests.name: The offline fallback is cached
tests.script: assert(/offline\.html/.test(text), 'Add offline.html to the cache and as the fallback.');

hints: Put the cache name and the shell list in constants at the top.
In the fetch handler, check the URL first: if it starts with /wp-json/, use network-first.
After each handler, register the worker once the page has loaded.
The offline fallback is the page the user sees, so make it useful.

blocks.html: The question
What is the hard part?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Direct polish precisely, with design tokens and spacing instructions.
  2. Decide when a CSS framework helps and when it costs too much.
  3. Run a cross-browser and device check.
  4. Run the replication test on your A2 spec.
  5. Complete a handover pack: README, runbook, decision record, retrospective.
  6. Defend your architecture and read a diff in the viva.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour Three polish requests, a framework comparison, cross-browser checks
Lab 2 hours Polish sprint, replication test, final submission check, viva readiness
Viva Booked slot 10 minutes, screen shared, code open
The lab deliverable
A final A2 submission, a replication test result, a handover pack, and viva readiness.
The situation
The app works. The client is happy. The last 20% is the difference between a demo and a product. Your job: polish precisely, test broadly, and hand over cleanly.
Round 1: Polish sprint (50 minutes)

1. Choose three precise polish changes from the critique and the client's priorities.
  2. Write each as a specific instruction: what, where, and the expected effect.
  3. Make one commit per change.
  4. Do not change the architecture. Polish only.
  5. Re-test on a phone after each change.

Done when: three changes are committed and the app still works.
Round 2: Replication test (30 minutes)

1. Create an empty folder outside the repo.
  2. Open a fresh agent session.
  3. Give it only SPEC.md v2 and the fact sheet.
  4. Build the app in the empty folder.
  5. Compare the replica with your app.
  6. Record the biggest gap in CRITIQUE.md under ## Replication test.

Done when: the gap is recorded and you can name the missing sentence.
Round 3: Final submission check (20 minutes)

• [ ] Front end deployed and reachable.
  • [ ] WordPress backend reachable, or a local demo plus .wpress export.
  • [ ] REST data displayed with loading and error states.
  • [ ] Installable app with an offline state.
  • [ ] Checks passing or failures documented.
  • [ ] Security review of one plugin or endpoint.
  • [ ] SPEC.md v2, DECISIONS.md, CRITIQUE.md, AI-USE.md.
  • [ ] README.md, runbook, sprint retrospective.
  • [ ] Regular commits across Modules 07-11.
  • [ ] Instructor added as a collaborator.
Round 4: Viva readiness (10 minutes)

1. Trace a request from the front end through the API to WordPress and back.
  2. Open a commit. Explain the diff.
  3. Defend one architecture decision: platform, front end, data or mobile.
  4. Answer: "What would you do differently with more time?"

Done when: you can defend the architecture without notes.

lessons.title: Checkpoint: the last 20 percent is the product

questions.prompt: What is a design token?
options: A named design value, such as a spacing step or a colour, reused across the UI
A password for the design tool
A one-off pixel value chosen per page
An icon file
questions.explanation: Tokens turn design decisions into a shared vocabulary. They make polish consistent and reviewable.

questions.prompt: Why use a spacing scale such as 4, 8, 16, 24, 32?
options: Consistent rhythm, and instructions a developer can follow precisely
More spacing is always better
It removes the need for a stylesheet
It makes every page the same
questions.explanation: A scale bounds the choices. "Use 16px" is testable; "make it breathe" is not.

questions.prompt: When does a CSS framework help?
options: When you need standard components and consistency, and the cost is acceptable
Always. A framework is the professional choice
Only when you cannot write CSS
Never. Frameworks are always bloat
questions.explanation: A framework buys speed and consistency. It costs bundle size, override work, and a look you may have to fight.

questions.prompt: What counts as a cross-browser and device check?
options: The tasks on a real phone, plus the browsers your users actually use
One run in Chrome on your laptop
A screenshot at desktop width
The HTML validator passing
questions.explanation: Your laptop is not the client's phone. Test the tasks where the customers are.

questions.prompt: What makes the A2 replication test valid?
options: A fresh session, an empty folder, and only SPEC.md v2 and the fact sheet
Your current chat and your deployed app
A classmate reading your code
Running the checks again
questions.explanation: The test measures the spec. The builder must have nothing else.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a handover pack?
options: README, runbook, decision record and retrospective
Only the source code
The chat transcript
The Lighthouse screenshot
questions.explanation: The next person needs to run it, deploy it, understand the decisions and know what you learned.

questions.prompt: In the viva, how do you trace a booking from the form to the dashboard?
options: Browser form, serverless function, REST API with a stored credential, WordPress, then the authenticated dashboard
Form, CSS, WordPress, browser
Dashboard, WordPress, form, function
The agent built it, so it works
questions.explanation: Name each hop, the credential, and who can read the data at each step.

blocks.html: The question
What would you recommend, and why?
Learning objectives

By the end of this module you can:

  1. Evaluate a technology on maturity, cost, lock-in, skills, risk and reversibility.
  2. Place technologies on an adopt, trial, assess and hold radar, with reasons.
  3. Read a vendor proposal and find the hidden cost.
  4. Write a recommendation memo for a non-technical board.
  5. Defend a recommendation under challenge.
  6. Prepare for the A3 take-home and viva.
This module

Component Time What happens
Lecture 1 hour Build a class tech radar, evaluate proposals, demonstrate the A3 viva
Lab 2 hours Mock scenario, mock memo, mock viva in pairs
The lab deliverable
A mock memo and a mock viva. The feedback is formative.
The situation

The board has two proposals for the relaunch: a WordPress agency and an AI site-builder subscription. The current site is flawed. The board is non-technical. You have one hour to audit it and recommend a path.
Round 1: Read the scenario (20 minutes)

1. Read the brief and the two proposals.
  2. List the board's three priorities.
  3. Find one contradiction or omission in each proposal.
  4. Write one question you would ask each vendor.

Done when: you can name the hidden cost in each proposal.
Round 2: Audit and memo (40 minutes)

In pairs:

  1. Audit the flawed site against the brief. Find five issues.
  2. Rate each issue: high, medium, low.
  3. Write a one-page memo to the board: - What is wrong, and why it matters. - What you would fix first. - Which proposal you recommend, with benefits, limitations and risks. - A known-issues register.
  4. Keep it under two pages. Concise is better.

Done when: the memo has a recommendation, not a summary.
Round 3: Mock viva (30 minutes)

In pairs, one examiner and one candidate. Swap after 15 minutes.

The examiner:

  1. Asks the candidate to defend the recommendation.
  2. Challenges one assumption.
  3. Names a fix and asks for the diff.
  4. Changes the brief: "The budget halves" or "they need bookings in two languages." Ask how the recommendation changes.

The candidate shares the screen and talks through the work.

Done when: the candidate can defend the recommendation under challenge.
Round 4: Feedback (20 minutes)

Give one thing that held up and one thing to fix. Use the A3 viva criteria:

Criterion What to look for
Recommendation reasoning Holds up under challenge; trade-offs named
Diff explanation Names what changed and why it works
Adaptation Adjusts the recommendation when the brief changes
Communication Clear, direct, no jargon for the board

questions.prompt: Which set is the technology evaluation criteria from this module?
options: Maturity, cost, lock-in, skills, risk, reversibility
Colour, animation, framework, version, stars, downloads
Speed, size, syntax, licence, author, date
Popularity, hype, conference talks, blog posts, age, logo
questions.explanation: Evaluate against the client and the maintenance reality, not the trend.

questions.prompt: What does the Adopt ring mean on a tech radar?
options: Proven enough to use now, with confidence
Interesting, but not yet understood
Use only in a timeboxed trial
Do not use
questions.explanation: Adopt is for technology you would use on a real project now. Trial, Assess and Hold follow.

questions.prompt: The AI builder is half the price of the agency. What is the hidden cost?
options: The three-year cost and the cost of leaving, not just the build
The cost of the domain
The cost of the office wifi
There is no hidden cost; the quote is the cost
questions.explanation: A cheap build can be expensive to maintain or leave. The board is buying a three-year outcome.

questions.prompt: The board is non-technical. How should the memo lead?
options: With the recommendation and the reason, then the evidence
With the full list of bugs
With the code diff
With the vendor's marketing copy
questions.explanation: The board needs a decision and its trade-offs. Evidence follows to support it.

questions.prompt: In the viva, the examiner says "the budget halves". What do you do?
options: Adjust the recommendation and name what you would drop or defer
Repeat the same recommendation word for word
Refuse to answer
Recommend the cheapest quote
questions.explanation: Adaptation is part of the assessment. Keep the priority, change the scope.

questions.prompt: A technology is new and popular. Is that a reason to adopt it?
options: No. Popularity is not evidence for this client's needs
Yes. Popular technology is always safer
Yes, if it has a large community
No, because new technology never works
questions.explanation: Evaluate maturity, cost, lock-in, skills, risk and reversibility for the brief.

questions.prompt: What is a known-issues register?
options: A list of accepted problems with severity and a plan or mitigation
A list of every bug in the backlog
A list of the team's mistakes
A list of the vendor's promises
questions.explanation: A known issue is a decision to ship with a problem, recorded with its risk and what you will do about it.

  • What we found: five issues, rated high, medium or low.
  • What we would fix first: an ordered list.
  • The proposals: compare build cost, three-year cost, who edits content, lock-in and hidden cost.
  • Recommendation: choose one, with benefits, limitations and risks.
  • Known issues: what you accept, with severity and a mitigation.

Lead with the decision. Keep it under 650 words. The board is not technical.
